cues.text: Lecture five moves to health, the most important application of nanomaterials.
Nanomaterials are used in all three sectors of health: prevention, diagnosis and treatment.
This lecture covers prevention, and starts on diagnosis.
The prevention slide says: the best way to eliminate the problem is to eliminate the cause.
Antibacterial, antiviral and antifungal nanoparticles go into masks, gloves, sprays and other personal protective equipment.
Notice the idea. Nano does not invent new materials here. It uses the same ones, like silver or gold, in nano size. Their higher reactivity kills pathogens better.
Personal care does the same: zinc oxide and titanium dioxide in sunscreen, and silver nanoparticles in antifungal shampoo and antibacterial textiles.
His warning: nanomaterials are still new. Their long-term effects, such as genotoxicity, are unknown. Use them with precautions, and with real certificates.
Why early diagnosis? The slide gives three reasons.
To choose the best therapeutic method, and stop the disease from progressing.
To increase the effectiveness of the treatment.
And to avoid wasting excess medical resources.
There are three categories of diagnostic techniques: imaging, biosensors, and wearable sensors.
This next part is a likely written question: ionizing versus non-ionizing radiation.
Non-ionizing radiation does not have enough energy to ionize our cells. Power lines, radio, mobile networks, infrared and visible light. It is safe.
Ionizing radiation, which means ultraviolet, X-rays and gamma rays, has enough energy to break molecular bonds. It is harmful.
So the techniques that use ionizing radiation are invasive. PET and SPECT use gamma rays. CT uses X-rays.
MRI, ultrasound and optical imaging use none of it. They are non-invasive.
Optical imaging uses light, which is non-ionizing. It can catch metabolic changes, early markers of disease.
Its weakness: light does not penetrate deep into the body.
Fluorescence imaging injects a dye, such as indocyanine green, that glows under near-infrared light. Because it is injected, it is called minimally invasive. But the dye goes everywhere.
Nanoparticles are better probes. Gold nanoparticles.
Upconversion nanoparticles: they absorb near-infrared light, which penetrates deep, and emit visible or ultraviolet light.
And quantum dots, with an excellent quantum yield and low photobleaching.
